$comment: Prioritised work. See engineering/README.md for priority and status conventions. Keep this deduplicated and honest — a backlog of a thousand generated items is a backlog nobody reads.

items.description: Wire bounded iteration into orchestrated runs, so a failed review drives a second generation attempt inside the run rather than only when iterateWithReview is called directly.
items.whyItMatters: Today an orchestrated run generates once and reviews once. The retry loop exists, is tested, and is unreachable from a real request — which means the autonomous-improvement behaviour the workspace UI can display cannot actually occur.
acceptanceCriteria: A run whose review fails produces a second attempt without a new user request
The attempt ceiling is enforced inside the run, not only inside iterateWithReview
Every attempt persists as an ArtifactVersion with lineage, including rejected ones
items.verificationCriteria: An acceptance test where the first review fails and the second passes, asserting exactly two provider calls and two persisted versions.
items.designNote: The executor runs a flat ordered step list; it has no loop construct. Either the orchestrator appends a retry step when a review fails (needs the executor to support dynamic step insertion), or a single step owns the whole loop internally. The second is smaller and keeps the executor unchanged — decide deliberately.

items.description: Poll submitted video jobs and close their CapabilityRun rows.
items.whyItMatters: submitVideo returns a job and leaves the CapabilityRun RUNNING forever. The trace therefore reports a run as permanently live, and no cost is ever recorded for video.
acceptanceCriteria: A completed provider job closes its CapabilityRun with status, duration and cost
A failed job records the failure reason
The trace stops reporting live once the job settles
items.verificationCriteria: Unit test with an injected video provider returning a terminal job status.

items.description: Route the chat entry point through the capability orchestrator so a conversational request can start a real run.
items.whyItMatters: The directive's target flow is USER -> BRAIN -> ROUTER -> ORCHESTRATOR -> EXECUTOR. Chat currently ends at a text response; only /agents and the API can start orchestrated work, so the main entry point cannot do the main thing.
acceptanceCriteria: A chat message that routes to a non-empty plan starts a run and returns its id
A message that routes to an empty plan still answers normally, with no AgentRun created
The response links to the workspace for the run
items.verificationCriteria: Integration test covering both branches; assert no AgentRun row for an ordinary question.

items.description: Suit asset lifecycle: catalog -> preview -> selected -> hero, so 60+ suits do not each hold hero-resolution resources.
items.whyItMatters: Directive section 22. Without a promotion/demotion lifecycle, scaling the catalogue degrades memory and frame rate on exactly the devices that matter most.
acceptanceCriteria: Only the active suit holds hero-fidelity resources
Deselecting a suit disposes its GPU resources
Switching suits does not grow memory monotonically
items.verificationCriteria: Measured before/after: resident GPU memory and suit-switch time across ten switches. Numbers recorded, not asserted from intuition.

items.description: Hands: five-finger definition, thumb opposition, fingernail plates.
items.whyItMatters: Hands are the second thing a viewer looks at after the mask, and currently read as mittens at close camera distances.
acceptanceCriteria: Five separated digits
Thumb opposes rather than sitting in the finger plane
Nail plates read at hero camera distance
items.verificationCriteria: Render at hero distance and inspect the image. Blender (bpy 5.0.1) must be reinstalled in a fresh container: pip install bpy==5.0.1.
items.note: Recorded lesson from earlier passes: a feature only reads by CONTRAST with its surroundings — scaling every sculpt field up together produces pouches, not detail.

items.description: Garment and fabric micro-detail: seam pressure, panel transitions, roughness variation that reads as technical textile rather than armour.
items.whyItMatters: Directive section 16 — the design language is ADVANCED TECHNICAL FABRIC, not armoured sci-fi. This is the difference.
acceptanceCriteria: Fabric reads as woven at hero distance
No moiré at any supported camera distance
items.verificationCriteria: Render and inspect. Respect the Nyquist clamp already in texturing.py — weave period must stay above ~5 texels or it aliases.
items.note: Recorded lesson: never derive a texture feature from a texture-space gradient. Adjacent texels are metres apart across UV seams; derive in world space.

items.description: Deterministic repository scanner that reports findings into this backlog without calling any model.
items.whyItMatters: Directive sections 34-38 want a free engineering shift that uses zero inference. The value is in what it detects deterministically: oversized assets, missing responsive variants, undisposed 3D resources, bundle regressions.
acceptanceCriteria: Runs offline with no API key and no model call
Appends deduplicated items to backlog.json rather than rewriting it
Only auto-fixes changes that are deterministic, reversible and test-verified; everything else becomes a needsOpus item
items.verificationCriteria: Run twice in succession — the second run must add nothing new. A scanner that regenerates its own findings is noise.
items.constraint: MUST NOT circumvent Anthropic usage limits, impersonate Claude, or substitute another paid model. Deterministic tooling and genuinely local tools only.

items.description: Establish measured baselines: JS bundle, 3D payload, initial load, suit-switch time.
items.whyItMatters: Directive section 32 — improvements cannot be claimed without measurement, and there is currently no baseline to compare against.
acceptanceCriteria: Baseline numbers recorded in engineering/state.json
Reproducible command documented
items.verificationCriteria: Two consecutive measurements agree within a stated tolerance.
